newsitem.title: UK: UK to submit plan for partial lifting of beef ban.
newsitem.headline: UK to submit plan for partial lifting of beef ban.

text.p: Britain will soon submit proposals for an initial relaxation of the ban on its beef exports imposed by the European Union last March because of fears of mad cow disease, Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg said on Monday.

Hogg told parliament he would formally submit proposals to the European Commission within a couple of weeks for the ban to be lifted on herds that are certified to be free of mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
Because of the low incidence of BSE in Northern Ireland and electronic tagging of cattle there, Hogg said a certified herd scheme would particularly benefit the province's beef farmers.
Hogg was speaking at the start of a debate called by the main opposition Labour party censuring the minister's handling of the mad cow crisis.

The ruling Conservatives, with no overall majority in the House of Commons, are increasingly dependent on the nine-strong Ulster Unionist Party, and there has been speculation that the UUP has wrung concessions from the government in return for its support in Monday's late-evening vote.
But Hogg, who dimissed Labour's motion as a cheap political stunt, said farmers throughout the United Kingdom, not just Northern Ireland, would benefit from a certified herd scheme.

He said Britain had fulfilled its part of the deal struck by Prime Minister John Major at last June's EU summit in Florence, aimed at a staged lifting of the ban, and was now entitled to look to its EU partners to meet their side of the bargain.
Evidence disclosed last year that mad cow disease could probably be transmitted to humans had led to British farming's gravest crisis ever, Hogg said.
But he said the government had put stringent health measures in place that meant British beef was now the safest in Europe.
Confirmed cases of BSE were falling at 40 percent a year and the disease would disappear from the national herd by around 2001, Hogg said.
"We have created the circumstances in which the British beef industry can face the future with confidence," he said.
